sensitivity_note: Classical myth, widely used in fiction. Unverified, one source.

license_note: Myth; public domain ideas, own description.

name: Taniwha
looks: Large water or cave beings that may look like a whale, shark, spined lizard, or a strange floating log.
behavior: Guard tribal places and punish broken tapu; stories also have them eating outsiders and abducting people.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Red as an enemy: many iwi regard taniwha as kaitiaki (guardians), and taniwha have shaped modern road and court decisions. The same source shows dangerous stories exist, but Te Ara returned HTTP 403, so I cannot show an iwi-sanctioned monster use. Unverified, one source.

name: Te Wheke-a-Muturangi
looks: A monstrous giant octopus.
behavior: A pet of the tohunga Muturangi that preyed on fishing grounds; chased by the ancestor Kupe across Cook Strait and killed with an adze.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Red until the owner decides: it is tied to named ancestors (Kupe, or Tamatea in another iwi's version), so it is an ancestor story with competing iwi versions. Te Ara not readable. Unverified, one source.
reads_at_16x20: yes: a big octopus is clear.

name: Patupaiarehe
looks: Pale, fair-haired people, no tattoos, who appear in mist; hurt by sunlight.
behavior: Live in hidden mountain and forest villages; sometimes hostile to intruders, sometimes peaceful. Hate fire and steam; give themselves away with music in fog.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Living iwi tradition that varies by tribe; stories were recorded by outside collectors. Use as a generic misty-forest fey, not tied to a named iwi, and take care with a pale-skinned design. Unverified, one source.
reads_at_16x20: no: easily reads as a villager unless given strong gear.

name: Kurangaituku
origin: Maori (Te Arawa, Raukawa), Aotearoa New Zealand
looks: A woman-bird with wings for arms, clawed fingers and a beak.
behavior: Keeps birds and lizards in a cave and chases the youth Hatupatu; she dies in boiling mud. Some tellings make her a gentle caretaker.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Told by specific iwi; versions disagree on whether she is a villain, and there are modern retellings by Maori authors. Benevolent in some tellings. Unverified, one source.

name: Rainbow Serpent
looks: A giant serpent linked to deep waterholes and rainbows.
behavior: Creator being that causes storms and drowning when angered and swallows and returns people in myths.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Red: a creator being worshipped in ritual across many nations. Listed so the owner sees it; do not use. Unverified, one source.

name: Bunyip
origin: Aboriginal Australia (Wemba-Wemba or Wergaia name, Victoria)
looks: Accounts vary: a shaggy seal- or dog-like beast, or a long-necked animal with an emu or horse head.
behavior: Lives in swamps and waterholes, roars at night, and is said to take people who stray near water. A Ngarrindjeri water spirit punishes over-fishing.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Default would be red. Yellow because the source shows the word has been in public print since 1845, was displayed in a museum in 1847, and is a general water-danger tale. I read no Aboriginal-authored source, so the owner should decide. Unverified, one source.

name: Yara-ma-yha-who
looks: A small red frog-like man with a huge head, wide toothless mouth and suckers on hands and feet.
behavior: Waits in fig trees, drops on travelers, drains their blood and swallows them, then spits them out shorter.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Default would be red. Yellow because it is a told-to-children cautionary tale appearing in a 1932 collection and in a book by the Ngarrindjeri author David Unaipon (as cited by the source). Owner should confirm. Unverified, one source.
reads_at_16x20: yes: small red suckered figure is distinct.

name: Yowie
origin: Aboriginal Australia (Gamilaraay name, NSW) and colonial reports
looks: A tall hairy ape-like biped with a flat nose.
behavior: Reclusive in some accounts, violent in others; reported in the Outback.
license_note: Cryptid; folklore age unverified as a monster (name recorded 1875, ape reports from the 1870s-80s). Own description.
sensitivity_note: Grew partly from an Aboriginal spirit name recorded by a colonist; the modern cryptid is mostly colonial. Use only as a generic ape-beast. Unverified, one source.

name: Moo
looks: Shapeshifting reptile spirits that may appear as monstrous lizards, geckos or people.
behavior: Control water and weather and dwell in fishponds; some are man-eaters slain by heroines.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Red: revered as aumakua (family guardians), and named moo guard places. Unverified, one source.

name: Adaro
looks: No set look; ghost adaro enter sharks, snakes, trees or stones.
behavior: Shark-adaro drag people from canoes; snake-adaro take a sleeper's soul and cause death.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Living beliefs of the Makira people recorded mostly by early outside ethnographers; a spirit-type adaro also appears in creation tales. Use only as a generic shark-spirit. Unverified, one source.
reads_at_16x20: yes if drawn as a shark.

name: Ahuizotl
looks: A dog-sized water beast with black rubbery fur, monkey-like hands and a tail ending in a hand.
behavior: Lives in deep pools, snatches people from the shore and takes eyes, nails and teeth; mimics a baby's cry to lure victims.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description. Described in the Florentine Codex per the source.
sensitivity_note: Tied to the rain gods; priests alone handled its dead. Many descendants keep Nahua tradition. Not worshipped itself. Unverified, one source.
reads_at_16x20: yes: tail-hand is a clear mark.

name: Tzitzimitl
looks: Skeletal women in skirts, star-linked.
behavior: Were said to descend during eclipses and devour people if the New Fire rite failed.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Red: celestial female deities tied to fertility and childbirth; post-conquest writers called them demons. Fits a cracked sky but must not be used. Unverified, one source.

name: Vucub Caquix
looks: A vain bird demon with shining eyes who claims to be the sun.
behavior: Perches in a tree and boasts; the Hero Twins shot him down and took his teeth, eyes and wealth.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description. Popol Vuh episode.
sensitivity_note: From the Popol Vuh, still a living K'iche' sacred text. The source calls him a demon, not a deity. Unverified, one source.
reads_at_16x20: yes: large bird with bright feathers.

name: Camazotz

behavior: Serves the underworld lords and takes the head of a hero.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description. Popol Vuh.
sensitivity_note: Popol Vuh is a living sacred text; the source calls it a spirit, not a major deity. Fit to Hollowspire is only the cave-bat feel. Unverified, one source.

name: Cipactli
looks: A primeval crocodile, fish and toad, with a mouth at every joint.
behavior: Always hungry; gods tore it apart to make the earth.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description.
sensitivity_note: Red: first day-sign of the sacred count and, in some versions, the earth deity. Unverified, one source.

name: Curupira
looks: A small brown forest spirit with backward feet; face traits vary by region.
behavior: Leads trackers astray, imitates calls and punishes those who overcut the forest.
license_note: Folklore; ideas public domain, own description. First recorded in a Jesuit letter, 1560.
sensitivity_note: Indigenous in origin, still told; mainly a forest guardian, but early sources feared it. Dangerous form exists. Unverified, one source.

name: Boitata
